records.text: They did find Gilgamesh, aka Nimrod.
records.speaker: Anonymous Source #1 (Ep QRS_hR7NXaQ)

appearances.snippet: You need to look up the research that was done by Rob Skiba. They did find Gilgamesh, aka Nimrod.

verification.notes: Transcript context identifies the asserted equation of Gilgamesh with Nimrod. Current scholarship treats Nimrod's historical identity as uncertain and does not identify him as Gilgamesh; the claim that archaeologists found Gilgamesh, also known as Nimrod, is unsupported and false as stated.

sources.title: Nimrod, Mighty Hunter and King - Who Was He?
sources.relevance: Scholarly review explains that Nimrod's identity is unresolved and does not establish Gilgamesh as Nimrod.

records.text: We invaded just after Gilgamesh was found.
records.speaker: Anonymous Source #1 (Ep QRS_hR7NXaQ)

appearances.snippet: Yes, we invaded just after he was found.

verification.notes: Transcript places the alleged discovery immediately before the 2003 invasion. A BBC report dated April 29, 2003 described a possible tomb match, after the March invasion began, while the underlying geophysical fieldwork occurred before the war. The chronology and certainty in the statement are therefore materially misleading.

sources.title: Gilgamesh tomb believed found
sources.relevance: April 29, 2003 report postdates the invasion and records only a tentative identification.

sources.title: Uruk - City of Gilgamesh: First tests in 2001 for magnetic prospecting
sources.relevance: Primary research paper establishes that the underlying prospecting began in 2001.

records.text: The first place that U.S. forces went during the Iraq War and set up a base was a museum that held relics, Babylonian cuneiform tablets, and Gilgamesh's tomb.
records.speaker: Anonymous Source #1 (Ep QRS_hR7NXaQ)

appearances.snippet: The first place that we went during that war and set up a base was a museum. Not just any museum, the museum that held all of the relics. licks for that. It also held all the cuneiform tablets from Babylon and Gilgamesh and or Nimrod's tomb.

verification.notes: Transcript asserts that the museum/relic site was the first destination and base of U.S. forces. Current institutional records show Camp Alpha was established at Babylon after the invasion, but do not show it was the first place U.S. forces went; the Gilgamesh work was at Uruk, a different site. The composite claim is false.

sources.title: Report on Damage Assessments in Babylon
sources.relevance: UNESCO documents the later military base at Babylon but does not support the first-destination allegation.

sources.title: German Archaeological Institute - Uruk (Warka)
sources.relevance: Official project page locates the Gilgamesh-related prospecting at Uruk, not the Babylon museum/base.
